To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
estrogen decreases fatty acid synthesis in the mammary gland of both male and female rats, but not in the liver of male or female rats.
estrogen treatment decreases the lipogenic capacity in normal and neoplasia mammary tissue of male and female rats whereas the lipogenic capacity is increased in liver.

estrogen increases the activity of thioseterase II, an important regulator of fatty acid biosynthesis, in both normal mammary glands and in hormone-responsive, transplantabie mammary tumors in female rats, but not in male rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of estrogen treatment on lipogenic activity, and the tissue specificity of this effect, in male and female rat liver and mammary tissue.
the regulation of the synthesis of fatty acids and their subsequent utilization in the mammary gland and liver of female and male rats.
the effect of sex steroids on the lipogenic capacity and the fatty acid synthetases of mammary gland.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

estrogen treatment increased lipogenesis in liver and decreased it in the hormone-responsive, neoplastic tissue of male rats, whereas the effect of the hormone on lipogenic activity was opposite in the normal and neoplasia tissues of female rats.
the effects of estrogen on lipogenesis were tissue specific, and the effects of estrogen in normal and neoplasia of female rats were different from those in male rats.
estrogen has a lipogenic effect on the female mammary gland and a lipolytic effect on liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

estrogen treatment increased the activity of an enzyme involved in medium chain fatty acid synthesis and decreased the activity of enzymes involved in the production of longer chain fatty acids in both normal and tumor tissue.

estrogen increases fatty acid synthesis by increasing the rate of synthesis of fatty acid synthetases and acetyl-Coa carboxylase and by increasing the capacity to synthesize medium-chain-length fatty acids by increasing the activity of thioseterase II in mammary tissue of male and female rats.
estrogen has a tissue specific effect on lipogenic activity and this effect is dependent upon the sex of the animal.
The main takeaway from our work is that
estrogen treatment in male rats is associated with increased lipogenic capacity in liver, mammary gland, and the hormone-responsive R3230AC mammary tumor.

estrogen treatment decreases the lipogenic capacity and activity of fatty acid synthetases in male and female rat mammary tissue, whereas the activity of this pathway is increased in male and female liver.
estrogen is a key driver of mammary fat pad development.
